title: The whole of life in six orders
hookLine: the Mishnah has six orders; Shas is their abbreviation
carry: it all belongs to one Torah

lines: A LONG ROW OF HEAVY VOLUMES.
cards: On a shelf in a house of study stands a long row of matching volumes, tall and heavy, with gold letters on the spines. Someone points at the whole row and calls it by one short word: Shas. You hear it elsewhere too.
A person who knows Shas. A celebration for finishing Shas. It sounds like a nickname, and in a way it is: two Hebrew letters, shin and samekh, standing in for two words.
Those two words are a map of the whole Mishnah.

teach.b: Shas. Shin for shishah, six. Samekh for sedarim, orders.
Six orders. The Mishnah, and the Talmud built on it, is arranged in six large sections, and Shas became a name for the whole thing. Here they are.
Zeraim, seeds: blessings and farming. Moed, appointed time: Shabbat, festivals and fasts. Nashim, women: marriage, divorce and vows.
Nezikin, damages: courts, property, harm, and the sayings of the fathers.
Kodashim, holy things: the Temple's offerings. Tohorot, purities: what makes a person or a thing pure or impure.
Students hold the list with a traditional trick: the first letters spell two little Hebrew words, z'man nakat, roughly, he took time. Now hear the list as a whole.

teach.h: A FIELD, A CALENDAR, A HOME, A COURT.
teach.b: It starts in a field, with food. Then the calendar, the weeks and the seasons. Then the home, between two people.
Then out to the neighbors, the market and the court. Then up to the Temple. And finally the body, the house, and what is pure.

teach.h: A MAP OF A WHOLE LIFE.
teach.b: Some readers hear a map of a whole life: what you eat, when you rest, whom you love, how you treat the person next door, how you come near to God. Nothing is left out as too ordinary.
A wedding, a pothole and a holy day sit on the same shelf, under one short word.

teach.h: IT ALL BELONGS TO ONE TORAH.
teach.b: That's the claim hidden in the abbreviation: it all belongs to one Torah.

how: Students learn the six orders by name, and when a person or a study group completes a tractate or the whole of Shas, they hold a siyum, a festive meal, and recite the hadran, which promises to return to what was learned.

s: Shas is a Hebrew word for book
it's two letters standing for shishah sedarim, six orders.
the six orders start in a field and end with purity
Zeraim, Moed, Nashim, Nezikin, Kodashim, Tohorot: seeds first, purities last.
the Mishnah keeps everyday matters out of its holy books
a wedding, a pothole and a holy day sit on the same shelf.

games.q: you've just finished the last page of Shas, after a long time of study. friends have gathered. what do people traditionally do?
o: hold a siyum and promise to return.
games.why: a siyum, a festive meal, with the hadran: words that promise to return to what was learned, and it to you.

practice: On each out-breath, say one name quietly: Zeraim, Moed, Nashim, Nezikin, Kodashim, Tohorot.

Go round again, slower, and let each name bring up one part of your own life: a meal, your calendar, someone you love, a neighbor, a quiet moment, your own body. Keep circling, gently, until the time is up.

wordCard.voice: Shas. Short for shishah sedarim, the six orders of the Mishnah, and a name for the whole Talmud built on them. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew abbreviation for shishah sedarim, שִׁשָּׁה סְדָרִים, six orders.

carryVoice: Your line: it all belongs to one Torah. Tomorrow, the first of the six orders: seeds. Rest well.
